danish.title: Femtende bog (1812–13) — Kapitel 5
paragraphs: I 1812 og 1813 blev Kutuzov åbent beskyldt for fejltagelser. Kejseren var utilfreds med ham. Og i en nyligt skrevet historie, forfattet efter allerhøjeste befaling, hævdes det, at Kutuzov var en udspekuleret hoflogner, skræmt af Napoleons navn, og at han ved sine fejl ved Krasnoje og Berezina berøvede den russiske hær den fuldstændige sejrs glans.*
* Historien om året 1812. Kutuzovs karakter og betragtninger over de utilfredsstillende resultater af slagene ved Krasnoje, af Bogdanovitj.

Sådan er skæbnen — ikke for store mænd (grands hommes), som den russiske tankegang ikke anerkender — men for de sjældne og altid ensomme personer, der erkender Forsynets vilje og underkaster deres egen vilje den. Mængdens had og foragt straffer sådanne mennesker for at have set de højere love.

For russiske historikere — det er underligt og forfærdeligt at sige — er Napoleon, dette mest ubetydelige redskab i historien, som aldrig nogen steder, ikke engang i landflygtighed, viste menneskelig værdighed, genstand for tilbedelse og begejstring; han er stor. Men Kutuzov — den mand, der fra begyndelse til ende af sin virksomhed i 1812, uden nogensinde at vakle med et ord eller en handling fra Borodino til Vilna, viste et enestående eksempel på selvopofrelse og nutidig bevidsthed om begivenhedernes fremtidige betydning — Kutuzov forekommer dem ubestemt og beklagelsesværdig, og når de taler om ham og om året 1812, er de altid lidt flove.

Alligevel er det svært at forestille sig en historisk skikkelse, hvis virke så urokkelig var rettet mod ét enkelt mål; og det ville være svært at forestille sig noget mål mere værdigt eller mere i samklang med hele folkets vilje. Endnu vanskeligere ville det være at finde et tilfælde i historien, hvor en historisk persons mål blev så fuldstændig opfyldt som det, Kutuzovs indsats var rettet mod i 1812.

Kutuzov talte aldrig om »fyrre århundreder, der skuede ned fra pyramiderne«, om de ofre, han bragte for fædrelandet, eller om hvad han agtede at udrette eller havde udrettet; han sagde overhovedet intet om sig selv, han indtog ingen pose, han fremstod altid som det enkleste og mest ordinære menneske og sagde de enkleste og mest ordinære ting. Han skrev breve til sine døtre og til Madame de Staël, læste romaner, nød selskab af smukke kvinder, spøgte med generaler, officerer og soldater og modsagde aldrig dem, der forsøgte at bevise noget for ham. Da grev Rostopchin (Rostoptjin) ved Jauza-broen galopperede hen til Kutuzov med personlige bebrejdelser for at have forårsaget Moskvas ødelæggelse og sagde: »Hvordan kunne De love ikke at opgive Moskva uden kamp?« svarede Kutuzov: »Og det gør jeg heller ikke« — skønt Moskva allerede var opgivet. Da Araktjejev kom til ham fra kejseren og sagde, at Jermolov burde udnævnes til artillerichef, svarede Kutuzov: »Ja, det sagde jeg netop selv« — skønt han et øjeblik forinden havde sagt det stik modsatte. Hvad betød det for ham — som alene, midt i en meningsløs folkemængde, forstod hele den uhyre betydning af det, der skete — hvad betød det for ham, om Rostopchin tilskrev Moskvas ulykker ham eller sig selv? Endnu mindre kunne det betyde noget for ham, hvem der blev udnævnt til artillerichef.

Ikke blot sagde den gamle mand i disse tilfælde, men altid, ting der var helt uden mening i sig selv — for han havde nået en erfaring i livet, der havde overbevist ham om, at tanker og de ord, der tjener som deres udtryk, ikke er det, der bevæger mennesker — han brugte sådanne intetsigende ord, fordi de tilfældigvis var ved hånden.

Men den mand, som var så skødesløs med sine ord, udtalte ikke én eneste gang i hele sin virketid et ord, der var i modstrid med det ene mål, han bevægede sig mod gennem hele krigen. Tilsyneladende mod sin vilje, under de mest forskellige omstændigheder, gav han gang på gang udtryk for sin sande overbevisning med den bitre forvisning, at han ikke ville blive forstået. Fra Slaget ved Borodino, hvorfra hans uenighed med sine omgivelser begyndte, sagde han alene, at Borodino var en sejr, og han gentog det både mundtligt og i sine depecher og rapporter til sin død. Han alene sagde, at Moskvas tab ikke er Ruslands tab. Da Lauriston foreslog fred, sagde han: Der kan ikke være fred, for det er folkets vilje. Han alene sagde under den franske tilbagetog, at alle vores manøvrer er unyttige, at alt sker af sig selv, bedre end vi kunne ønske; at fjenden skal tilbydes en »gylden bro«; at hverken Tarutino-, Vjazma- eller Krasnoje-slagene var nødvendige; at vi må bevare nogen styrke for at nå grænsen med, og at han ikke ville ofre en eneste russer for ti franskmænd.

Og han alene — denne hofmand, som man beskriver os, han der lyver for Araktjejev for at behage kejseren — han alene vovede i Vilna at sige, skønt det mishagede kejseren, at det ville være skadeligt og meningsløst at føre krigen videre over grænsen.

Det er ikke ordene alene, der beviser, at kun han forstod begivenhedernes mening. Hans handlinger — uden den mindste afvigelse — var alle rettet mod ét og det samme trefoldige mål: (1) at samle al sin styrke til kampen mod franskmændene, (2) at besejre dem, og (3) at drive dem ud af Rusland, idet han så vidt muligt mindskede lidelserne for vores folk og vores hær.

Denne nølende Kutuzov, hvis motto var »Tålmodighed og tid«, denne fjende af afgørende handling, gav slag ved Borodino og omgav forberedelserne med en uhørt højtidelighed. Denne Kutuzov, som før Austerlitz sagde, at slaget ville gå tabt, han alene erklærede — i modstrid med alle andre — til sin død, at Borodino var en sejr, trods generalernes forsikringer om, at slaget var tabt, og trods det forhold, at det var uhørt, at en hær måtte trække sig tilbage efter at have vundet. Han alene insisterede under hele tilbagetrækningen på, at slag, der nu var nytteløse, ikke skulle udkæmpes, og at en ny krig ikke skulle begyndes og Ruslands grænser ikke overskrides.

Det er nu let at forstå disse begivenheders betydning — hvis blot vi afstår fra at tillægge massernes handlinger mål, der kun fandtes i hovederne på et dusin enkeltpersoner — for begivenhederne og deres resultater ligger åbent for os.
Men hvordan kunne den gamle mand, alene og i modstrid med den almene opfattelse, så sandt erkende begivenhedernes folkelige betydning, at han i al sin virksomhed aldrig én gang var den utro?
Kilden til denne usædvanlige evne til at gennemtrænge de igangværende begivenheders mening lå i den nationale følelse, som han besad i sin fulde renhed og styrke.

Kun erkendelsen af, at han besad denne følelse, fik folket til på så mærkelig vis, i modstrid med tsarens ønske, at vælge ham — en gammel mand i unåde — som sin repræsentant i den nationale krig. Og kun den følelse placerede ham på den højeste menneskelige piedestal, hvorfra han som øverstkommanderende viede al sin kraft ikke til at slå ihjel og ødelægge, men til at redde og vise barmhjertighed.
Den enkle, beskedne og derfor virkelig store skikkelse kunne ikke passes ind i den falske form af en europæisk helt — den påståede hersker over mennesker — som historien har opfundet.
For en lakaj kan intet menneske være stort, for en lakaj har sit eget begreb om storhed.

english.title: Book Fifteen (1812 - 13) — Chapter 5
paragraphs: In 1812 and 1813, Kutuzov was openly accused of blundering. The Emperor was dissatisfied with him. And in a history recently written by official command, it is stated that Kutuzov was a cunning court liar, terrified of Napoleon's name, and that by his blunders at Krasnoe and the Berezina he deprived the Russian army of the glory of a complete victory over the French.
(History of the Year 1812. The character of Kutuzov and reflections on the unsatisfactory results of the battles at Krasnoe, by Bogdanovich.)

Such is the fate—not of great men ("grands hommes") as the Russian mind does not acknowledge them—but of those rare and always solitary individuals who, perceiving the will of Providence, submit their personal will to it. The hatred and contempt of the crowd is the punishment for those who discern a higher law.

For Russian historians, strange and terrible to say, Napoleon—that most insignificant tool of history, who never anywhere, even in exile, showed human dignity—Napoleon is the object of admiration and enthusiasm; he is "grand." But Kutuzov—the man who from beginning to end of his activity in 1812 never once wavered by word or deed from Borodino to Vilna, who presented an example of self-sacrifice unmatched in history and a living awareness of the future significance of what was happening—Kutuzov seems to them something vague and pathetic, and when they speak of him and of the year 1812, they always seem a little embarrassed.

And yet it is hard to imagine a historical figure whose actions were so unwaveringly directed toward a single aim. And it would be hard to imagine any aim more worthy or more in harmony with the will of the entire people. Still harder would it be to find another instance in history where the aim of a historical figure was so completely accomplished as the aim to which all of Kutuzov's efforts were directed in 1812.

Kutuzov never spoke of "forty centuries looking down from the Pyramids," of the sacrifices he was making for the fatherland, or of what he intended or had accomplished. In general he said nothing about himself, struck no poses, always appeared to be the simplest and most ordinary of men, and said the simplest and most ordinary things. He wrote letters to his daughters and to Madame de Stael, read novels, enjoyed the company of pretty women, joked with generals, officers, and soldiers, and never contradicted anyone who tried to prove anything to him. When Count Rostopchin galloped up to Kutuzov at the Yauza bridge and personally accused him of causing Moscow's destruction, saying: "How could you promise not to abandon Moscow without a battle?" Kutuzov replied: "And I shall not abandon Moscow without a battle"—though Moscow was already abandoned. When Arakcheev, coming from the Emperor, told him that Ermolov ought to be appointed chief of artillery, Kutuzov replied: "Yes, I was just saying so myself"—though a moment before he had said the exact opposite. What did it matter to him—the only man amid a senseless crowd who understood the tremendous significance of what was happening—whether Rostopchin blamed him or himself for Moscow's destruction? Still less could it matter who was named chief of artillery.

Not only in these cases but constantly, that old man—who through long experience had reached the conviction that thoughts and the words expressing them are not what move people—used perfectly meaningless words that simply came into his head.

But that man, so careless with his words, never once during his entire period of activity uttered a single word inconsistent with the one aim toward which he worked throughout the whole war. Obviously, despite himself, in the most diverse circumstances, he repeatedly expressed his true convictions with the bitter certainty that he would not be understood. Beginning with the battle of Borodino, from which point his disagreement with those around him began, he alone said that Borodino was a victory, and he repeated this both verbally and in his dispatches and reports until his death. He alone said that the loss of Moscow did not mean the loss of Russia. In reply to Lauriston's proposal of peace, he said: There can be no peace, for such is the people's will. He alone, during the French retreat, said that all their maneuvers were useless, that everything was working out better than they could wish without them, that the enemy must be offered a "golden bridge," that the battles at Tarutino, Vyazma, and Krasnoe were unnecessary, that they needed to keep enough strength to reach the border, and that he would not sacrifice a single Russian for ten Frenchmen.

And this courtier, as he is portrayed—who lies to Arakcheev to please the Emperor—he alone, at the cost of the Emperor's displeasure, said in Vilna that to carry the war beyond the frontier was useless and harmful.

Nor do his words alone prove that he understood the meaning of events. His actions—without the slightest deviation—were all directed toward one and the same threefold end: (1) to concentrate all his strength for the conflict with the French, (2) to defeat them, and (3) to drive them out of Russia, while minimizing as far as possible the suffering of his people and his army.

This supposed procrastinator Kutuzov, whose motto was "Patience and Time," this supposed enemy of decisive action, gave battle at Borodino and invested the preparations for it with unparalleled solemnity. This Kutuzov, who before the battle of Austerlitz said it would be lost, he alone, contradicting everyone else, declared to his dying day that Borodino was a victory—despite the assurance of generals that the battle was lost and the unprecedented fact that an army had to retreat after winning. He alone, throughout the entire retreat, insisted that further battles were useless, that a new war should not be begun, and that the Russian frontier should not be crossed.

It is easy now to understand the significance of these events—if only we refrain from attributing to the actions of the masses aims that existed only in the heads of a dozen people—for the events and their results now lie before us.
But how did that old man, alone, in opposition to the general opinion, so accurately perceive the importance of the people's view of events that in all his actions he was never once untrue to it?
The source of that extraordinary power of insight lay in the national feeling that he possessed in full purity and strength.

Only the recognition that he possessed this feeling caused the people, in such a strange manner and contrary to the Tsar's wish, to choose him—an old man in disfavor—as their representative in the national war. And only that feeling placed him on the highest pedestal from which he, the commander in chief, devoted all his powers not to slaying and destroying men but to saving them and showing them pity.
That simple, modest, and therefore truly great figure could not be forced into the false mold of a European hero—the supposed ruler of men—that history has fabricated.
To a servant, no man can be great, because a servant has his own idea of what greatness means.
